translationRepairs: The court called him to be chief clerk and major under the minister of state and palace censor, then director of the Department of State Affairs, with a village marquisate at An'guo.

The court summoned him as Major to the Minister of State, Chief Clerk, and Palace Assistant Censor, then promoted him to Director of the Department of State Affairs and enfeoffed him as Marquis of An'guo Village.

The Chinese lists three successive offices (相國司馬, 長史, 御史中丞) before 遷尚書 and 封安國亭侯; the old idiomatic line fused them into an unclear pair of posts. The replacement names the three offices, the promotion, and the village marquisate accurately.
When his brother Zhi feuded with nephew Yu and aired lurid tales about Qian's sons and daughters, Qian used a memorial to exile Zhi—earning widespread scorn.
When his younger brother Zhi quarreled with Qian's son Yu, Zhi then spread scandal about the misconduct of Qian's children; Qian memorialized to have his brother banished, and was ridiculed for it.

弟稚與其子輿 names Yu as 其子 in this biography of Chen Qian, and s0047 子輿嗣爵 confirms Yu as Qian's son. The old idiomatic 'nephew Yu' made Yu Zhi's son; the replacement restores uncle and brother's-son as Zhi versus Qian's son.
His younger brother Zhi quarreled with Zhi's son Yu, then spread scandal about the misconduct of Qian's children; Qian memorialized to have his brother banished, and the world ridiculed him for it.
His younger brother Zhi quarreled with Qian's son Yu, then spread scandal about the misconduct of Qian's children; Qian memorialized to have his brother banished, and the world ridiculed him for it.
The old literal made 其子輿 into Zhi's son, contradicting 子輿嗣爵. 其 here tracks the biographical subject; the replacement correctly makes Yu Qian's son.
The marquisate passed to his son Yu.
The noble title passed to his son Yu.
嗣爵 is succession to Qian's noble rank, not specifically a marquisate. The burial in 袞斂 already marks a rank above a village marquis; 'noble title' matches 爵 without inventing a marquisate.
When Liu Yu accepted the Jin abdication, the marquisate was abolished.
When Song accepted the abdication, the fief was abolished.
宋受禪，國除 names only Song's receipt of abdication and abolition of the fief. The old literal invented the personal name Liu Yu, which is not in the unit.

General Who Crosses the Liao Guanqiu Jian once recommended Xiu to Great General Cao Shuang, saying, "Born extraordinary and lofty, growing up he trod what was natural, was profound and still, guarded truth, and by nature entered the depths of the Way.

General Who Crosses the Liao, Guanqiu Jian, once recommended Xiu to Great General Cao Shuang, saying, "Born extraordinary and lofty, growing up he trod what was natural, was profound and still, guarded truth, and by nature entered the depths of the Way.
渡遼將軍 is the office title and 毌丘儉 the personal name. Without a comma the English fuses them into one string; the commas restore the two constituents.
When Sima Zhao still hesitated over the succession, his eye rested on Prince You of Wuyang.
When Sima Zhao still hesitated over the succession, his eye rested on the Marquis of Wuyang, You.
舞陽侯攸 is a district marquis, not a prince. The replacement restores 侯.
That endorsement fixed Yan as heir.
由是世子乃定 settles the heir-apparent and does not name Yan. The old idiomatic line invented the personal name.
The new emperor hailed Pei's aid as rivaling the ancient worthies Gaoyuan and Kai.
The new emperor hailed Pei's aid as matching the deeds of the Yuan and Kai worthies.
配蹤元凱 alludes to the Yuan and Kai worthies (八元八凱), not a person named Gaoyuan plus Kai. The replacement restores that pair.
The court ordered Yi to succeed; he refused repeatedly yet had to accept.
An edict ordered Yi to inherit the noble rank; Yi firmly declined, but permission to decline was refused.
不許 means the court refused permission to decline 襲爵, not that Yi then accepted of his own accord. The replacement keeps the court's refusal.
When Xun Xiu revised pitch pipes and measures, inspection recovered an ancient foot shorter than those in current use by more than one fourth.
When Xun Xu revised pitch pipes and measures, inspection recovered an ancient foot shorter than those in current use by more than one fourth.
荀勖 is Xun Xu; the old literal's Xun Xiu is a false spelling. The replacement matches the name used in the surrounding units.

Because Empress Jia disliked the crown prince, Yi submitted a blunt memorial asking to elevate the rank title of Consort Xie who bore the heir, and further requested adding rear-guard officers for the heir's household with three thousand troops—thereupon the Eastern Palace had ten thousand household guards overnight.

Because Empress Jia disliked the crown prince, Yi submitted a blunt memorial asking to elevate the rank title of Consort Xie who bore the heir, and further requested adding rear-guard officers for the heir's household with three thousand troops—thereupon the Eastern Palace household guards numbered ten thousand.
東宮宿衛萬人 means the Eastern Palace household guards numbered ten thousand. 宿衛 is the guard corps, not the English adverb 'overnight'.
Where should I run?" Yu asked."
吾何之 is 'where shall I go?', not 'run'. The old idiomatic line also broke the quotation marks. The replacement restores Liu Yu's question.
Yi despised how fashion praised He Yan and Ruan Ji for idle chatter that ignored ritual while they pocketed salaries and neglected duty.

Yi deeply worried that the age's unrestrained customs did not honor Confucian teaching. He Yan and Ruan Ji enjoyed lofty reputations, talking idle emptiness and ignoring ritual law, drawing salary and indulging favor while holding office yet doing nothing.

深患時俗放蕩，不尊儒術 is Pei Wei's worry about unrestrained custom and neglect of Confucian teaching, then a separate indictment of He Yan and Ruan Ji. The old line collapsed that grammar into fashion praising the two men.
How much more is this true for one who occupies honor among the Three, holds feelings about what should be exalted, and treats them seriously as instruction.
How much more is this true for one who occupies the honor of the three (ruler, father, and teacher), holds feelings about what should be exalted, and treats them seriously as instruction.
The old 'the Three' is opaque, but the proposed 'three bonds' imports 三綱. 在三之尊 is the Guoyu triad of ruler, father, and teacher, not the three bonds.
How much more is this true for one who occupies honor among the Three, holds feelings about what should be exalted, and treats them seriously as instruction.
How much more is this true for one who occupies the honor of the three (ruler, father, and teacher), holds feelings about what should be exalted, and treats them seriously as instruction.
The literal shares the same false 'Three' as a proper name, and 'three bonds' is still the wrong allusion. 在三 is ruler, father, and teacher.
The qingtan circle attacked his thesis from every side without refuting it.
Wang Yan's clique besieged him with objections, yet none could break his argument.
王衍之徒 names Wang Yan's clique as the attackers. The old 'qingtan circle' erased that name and invented a school label.
Liang and Donghai princes cited Xiu's temple honors to spare the sons, exiling them to Liaodong instead.

Princes Sima Rong of Liang and Sima Yue of Donghai declared that Yi's father Xiu had served the dynasty and received offerings in the Grand Temple—his line must not be extinguished—so the boys lived on, banished to Daifang.
徙帶方 is banishment to Daifang, not Liaodong, and 梁王肜 is Sima Rong, not Yong. The proposed expansion of the princes' plea is otherwise faithful.
Adopted heir Gai died beside Song when Chen Wu's refugee warriors slaughtered them.
Gai had been adopted out to his father's cousin Kai; he was supernumerary attendant until both brothers fell to Chen Wu's Qi Huo band.
出後從伯凱 is a living adoption of Gai out to his father's cousin Kai, not a posthumous 'adopted heir'. The replacement also restores 散騎常侍 and 乞活賊陳午.
Father Pei Wei governed Ji province for Wei.
His father Hui had been Governor of Jizhou under Wei.
父徽 is Hui, not Wei. The old idiomatic line misread 徽 as Wei, colliding with the dynastic name 魏 in the same sentence.

Kai's heir Yu had married Sima Liang's daughter while Yu's wife joined Wei Guan's son—fearing civil war Kai sought a province; made southern commander with staff for Jingzhou—just as he prepared to march, Wei forged an edict killing Liang and Guan.

Kai's heir Yu had first married Sima Liang's daughter, and Kai's daughter was married to a son of Wei Guan—fearing civil war Kai sought a province; made General Who Pacifies the South, with staff, commanding Jingzhou military affairs—just as he prepared to march, Wei forged an edict killing Liang and Guan.
楷長子輿先娶亮女，女適衛瓘子 makes the second marriage Kai's daughter to Wei Guan's son, not Yu's wife. The replacement also restores 安南將軍、假節、都督荊州諸軍事.
He died the same year at fifty-five as Marquis Yuan.
That year he died, aged fifty-five; posthumous title Yuan.
諡曰元 is a posthumous name, not death 'as Marquis Yuan'. The replacement separates the death age from the posthumous title.
He succeeded early, died as supernumerary gentleman Jian.
In youth he inherited his father's noble rank, reached Supernumerary Gentleman of the Palace, and on death received the posthumous title Jian.
少襲父爵，官至散騎侍郎，卒諡曰簡 distinguishes inherited rank, the office 散騎侍郎, and posthumous 簡. The old line omitted the rank and fused office with the epithet Jian.
Guobao Zan awed onlookers from the palace secretariat.
Zan, whose courtesy name was Guobao, was Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat; his bearing was lofty, and all who saw him revered him.
瓚字國寶 gives the given name first, then the courtesy name, then 中書郎 and 風神高邁. The old line reversed name order and collapsed office and bearing into 'awed onlookers'.
Wang Sui especially esteemed him and constantly accompanied him on outings.
特為王綏所重，每從其遊 is that Wang Sui especially esteemed Zan and accompanied him. 'Shadowed' drops the honor relation 所重.
Wang Rong wondered why Sui chased a host who never called."
Sui's father Rong said to him: "Guobao never comes to you—why do you go to him so often?"
綏父戎謂之曰 records Wang Rong's quoted question to Sui about Guobao never coming. The old line garbled the quotation, invented 'host', and left a stray quote mark.
Jun's purge left Zan dead among the soldiers.
When Yang Jun was executed, Zan was killed by mutinous troops.
楊駿之誅，為亂兵所害 makes Yang Jun the one executed; Zan is killed by chaotic troops in that crisis, not by 'Jun's purge'.
Prince Donghai Yue made him Governor of Yuzhou, General Who Pacifies the North, and Bearer of Staff of Authority.
Prince of Donghai Yue made him Governor of Yuzhou, General of the Household of the North, and Bearer of the Staff of Authority.
北中郎將 is not 平北將軍. The proposed office is right, but the parenthetical 'Northern Zhonglangjiang' is awkward in running English.
Under Yuan-di Shao served with Wang Dao as the prince's twin pillars.
When Emperor Yuan was General of the East, he appointed Shao as chief clerk and Wang Dao as Sima; the two became close friends.

元帝為安東將軍，以邵為長史，王導為司馬，二人相與為深交 names Emperor Yuan's eastern generalship, Shao as chief clerk, Wang Dao as Sima, and their deep friendship. The old line fused Yuan-di with Shao and invented 'twin pillars'.
Wei-Jin society paired eight Peis with eight Wangs like paired stars.

The Pei and Wang houses flourished in the Wei-Jin age; contemporaries likened eight Peis to eight Wangs: Hui to Wang Xiang, Kai to Wang Yan, Kang to Wang Sui, Chuo to Wang Cheng, Zan to Wang Dun, Xia to Wang Dao, Yi to Wang Rong, and Miao to Wang Xuan.
The old sentence dropped the eight named pairings, and 王玄雲 is Wang Xuan plus the particle 雲. The proposed list is otherwise right, but 徽 is Hui, not Wei.
They hint Chen Qian embodied vain ministerial boasting.
When famous men were few, people mostly praised one another for administrative talent—glorifying house and state—is this not a description of Chen Qian!
豈陳騫之謂歟 asks whether the preceding portrait is said of Chen Qian, not that Chen Qian 'meant' something or merely embodied vain boasting. The replacement restores that rhetorical identification.

The court summoned him as Major to the Minister of State, Chief Clerk, and Palace Assistant Censor, then promoted him to Director of the Department of State Affairs and enfeoffed him as Marquis of An'guo Village.
The court summoned him as Major to the Minister of State, Chief Clerk, and Palace Assistant Censor, then promoted him to Imperial Secretary and enfeoffed him as Marquis of An'guo Village.
遷尚書 names the Shangshu / Imperial Secretary post, not 尚書令 (Director of the Department of State Affairs). The proposed untranslated 'Shangshu' is accurate in rank but not natural idiomatic English.

Chen Yu, style Xianchu, rose through supernumerary gentleman and Luoyang magistrate to palace attendant, then led the left colonel's corps, ran the Ministry of Agriculture, and returned to the palace corps.

Yu, courtesy name Xianchu, was appointed Cavalier Gentleman-in-Attendance and Magistrate of Luoyang, promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, then served successively as colonel of the Left Army, Minister of Agriculture, and Palace Attendant.
遷黃門侍郎 is promotion to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, not 侍中; 侍中 comes last. 厲將校左軍、大司農、侍中 is successive office-holding, not leading a colonel's corps then returning to a palace corps.
Shuang took him on staff; Xiu succeeded to the Qingyang village fief and entered the palace corps.
Shuang therefore summoned him as an aide; Xiu inherited his father's Qingyang village marquisate and was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
遷黃門侍郎 is promotion to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate; 'entered the palace corps' conflates it with 侍中 and omits the actual office.
Shuang therefore summoned him as an aide; Xiu inherited his father's Qingyang village marquisate and was promoted to Palace Attendant.
Shuang therefore summoned him as an aide; Xiu inherited his father's Qingyang village marquisate and was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
The literal likewise renders 黃門侍郎 as Palace Attendant (侍中); Gentleman of the Yellow Gate is the correct office.

He was summoned to serve as Major to the Minister of State, Chief Clerk, and Palace Assistant Censor, then promoted to Director of the Department of State Affairs and enfeoffed as Marquis of the An'guo village.
He was summoned to serve as Major to the Minister of State, Chief Clerk, and Palace Assistant Censor, then promoted to Shangshu and enfeoffed as Marquis of the An'guo village.
遷尚書 is the Shangshu post, not 尚書令. Leaving Shangshu in the literal column correctly distinguishes the later Director appointment.
When the emperor campaigned against Zhuge Dan, Xiu accompanied Minister of the Left Chen Tai and Palace Attendant Zhong Hui with the mobile headquarters staff and took part in strategic planning.

When the emperor campaigned against Zhuge Dan, Xiu accompanied Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Chen Tai and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Zhong Hui with the mobile headquarters staff and took part in strategic planning.
尚書僕射陳泰 is Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, not Minister of the Left; 黃門侍郎鍾會 is Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, not Palace Attendant.
When Dan was suppressed, Xiu was transferred to Director of the Department of State Affairs, advanced to Marquis of the Luyang district, with an additional thousand households.
When Dan was suppressed, Xiu was transferred to be a Shangshu, advanced to Marquis of the Luyang district, with an additional thousand households.
轉尚書 is transfer to a Shangshu post. 尚書令 appears only later (武帝既即王位，拜尚書令), so Director of the Department of State Affairs overstates the office.

When the Duke of Changdao was enthroned, Xiu shared in the preliminary council that fixed the succession; he was advanced to county marquis with seven hundred more households and promoted to Minister of the Left.

When the Duke of Changdao was enthroned, Xiu shared in the preliminary council that fixed the succession; he was advanced to county marquis with seven hundred more households and promoted to Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
遷尚書僕射 is promotion to Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat; the Chinese does not specify left 僕射 (Minister of the Left).

After Emperor Wu had taken the position of king, he appointed Pei Xiu Secretariat Director and Right Guanglu Grandee. Together with Censor-in-chief Wang Shen and General Who Guards Jia Chong, Pei Xiu opened an office, and he was additionally made Palace Attendant.

After Emperor Wu had taken the position of king, he appointed Pei Xiu Secretariat Director and Right Guanglu Grandee. Together with Censor-in-chief Wang Shen and General Who Guards Jia Chong, Pei Xiu opened an office, and he was additionally made Given Attendance within the Palace.
加給事中 is a concurrent Given Attendance within the Palace, not 侍中 (Palace Attendant).

After Emperor Wu had taken the position of king, he appointed Pei Xiu Secretariat Director and Right Guanglu Grandee. Together with Censor-in-chief Wang Shen and General Who Guards Jia Chong, Pei Xiu opened an office, and he was additionally made Palace Attendant.

After Emperor Wu had taken the position of king, he appointed Pei Xiu Secretariat Director and Right Guanglu Grandee. Together with Censor-in-chief Wang Shen and General Who Guards Jia Chong, Pei Xiu opened an office, and he was additionally made Given Attendance within the Palace.
The literal repeats the same 給事中 / Palace Attendant confusion; Given Attendance within the Palace matches the Chinese office.
The dull illegitimate Jing received a minor Gaoyang village marquisate while the legitimate junior uncle Yi took the primary succession.
Jun's dull-witted son by a concubine, Jing, was separately enfeoffed as Marquis of the Gaoyang village, and Jun's younger brother Yi succeeded to the main line.
浚庶子憬 is Jun's son by a concubine, separately enfeoffed; 以浚少弟頠嗣 makes Jun's younger brother Yi the main-line heir. 'Legitimate junior uncle' is invented kinship.
As Yang Jun fell, Liu Yu—Jun's colonel of the left—blocked the gate and demanded Sima Liang's whereabouts.
When Yang Jun was about to be executed, Jun's partisan General of the Left Army Liu Yu deployed troops at the gate; he met Yi and asked where the Grand Tutor was.
The sentence is 遇頠，問太傅所在: Liu Yu met Yi and asked for the Grand Tutor. The original omits that meeting and invents the personal name Sima Liang, which the Chinese does not give.
Yi lied that he had seen the grand tutor leave west through the western portal in a plain cart."
Yi lied that he had seen the grand tutor leave west through the Western Lateral Gate in a plain cart.
The stray closing quote is not in the Chinese. 西掖門 is the Western Lateral Gate, not a generic western portal.

At the time, Chen Zhun's son Kuang and Han Wei's son Song were both serving in the Eastern Palace. Wei remonstrated, saying, "The establishment of the Eastern Palace is to store up the imperial standard.

At the time, Chen Zhun's son Kuang and Han Wei's son Song were both serving in the Eastern Palace. Wei remonstrated, saying, "The Eastern Palace is established to uphold the heir as the imperial pole.
以儲皇極 means the Eastern Palace exists to hold the heir as the imperial pole (儲 = heir). 'Store up the imperial standard' misreads 儲 as 'store'.

Yi deeply worried that the age's unrestrained customs did not honor Confucian teaching. He Yan and Ruan Ji enjoyed lofty reputations, talking idle emptiness and ignoring ritual law, drawing salary and indulging favor while holding office yet doing nothing.

Pei Wei deeply worried that the age's unrestrained customs did not honor Confucian teaching. He Yan and Ruan Ji enjoyed lofty reputations, talking idle emptiness and ignoring ritual law, drawing salary and indulging favor while holding office yet doing nothing.
頠 here is the same man named Pei Wei in the following treatise sentence. Rendering him as Yi in this unit splits one person across two English names; the given name is Wei, not Yi.

Yi deeply worried that the customs of the age were unrestrained and did not honor Confucian teaching; He Yan and Ruan Ji enjoyed lofty reputations in the world, talking idle emptiness at the mouth and not observing ritual law—drawing salary and indulging favor while holding office yet doing nothing.

Pei Wei deeply worried that the customs of the age were unrestrained and did not honor Confucian teaching; He Yan and Ruan Ji enjoyed lofty reputations in the world, talking idle emptiness at the mouth and not observing ritual law—drawing salary and indulging favor while holding office yet doing nothing.
The literal likewise calls 頠 'Yi' while the next owned unit already uses Pei Wei for the same subject.

Princes Sima Yong of Liang and Sima Yue of Donghai declared that Yi's father Xiu had served the dynasty and received offerings in the Grand Temple—his line must not be extinguished—so the boys lived on, banished to Daifang.

Princes Sima Rong of Liang and Sima Yue of Donghai declared that Yi's father Xiu had served the dynasty and received offerings in the Grand Temple—his line must not be extinguished—so the boys lived on, banished to Daifang.
梁王肜 is Sima Rong (肜). Sima Yong would be a different prince (typically 顒) and is not in this sentence.
Gai had been posthumously adopted to uncle Kai; he was supernumerary attendant until both brothers fell to Chen Wu's Qi Huo band.
Gai had been adopted out to his father's cousin Kai; he was supernumerary attendant until both brothers fell to Chen Wu's Qi Huo band.
出後從伯凱 is adoption out during life to his father's cousin Kai, not a posthumous adoption and not a simple paternal uncle.
His father Wei had been Governor of Jizhou under Wei.
His father Hui had been Governor of Jizhou under Wei.
父徽 is Hui. The original 'father Wei' confuses the personal name 徽 with the polity 魏 in 魏冀州刺史.
He built a villa; cousin Wang Yan coveted it, so Kai gave him the house outright.
He built a villa; his elder cousin Yan coveted it, so Kai gave him the house outright.
從兄衍 is Kai's elder cousin Yan. The Chinese does not surname him Wang; 'cousin Wang Yan' invents an identity the source does not state.
眾人為之震恐 is the people present who were terrified. Luoyang is not in the Chinese.

At first the Pei and Wang houses flourished side by side in the Wei-Jin age; contemporaries likened eight Peis to eight Wangs: Wei to Wang Xiang, Kai to Wang Yan, Kang to Wang Sui, Chuo to Wang Cheng, Zan to Wang Dun, Xia to Wang Dao, Yi to Wang Rong, and Miao to Wang Xuanyun.

At first the Pei and Wang houses flourished side by side in the Wei-Jin age; contemporaries likened eight Peis to eight Wangs: Hui to Wang Xiang, Kai to Wang Yan, Kang to Wang Sui, Chuo to Wang Cheng, Zan to Wang Dun, Xia to Wang Dao, Yi to Wang Rong, and Miao to Wang Xuan.
徽比王祥 is Hui, not Wei. 邈比王玄雲 pairs Miao with Wang Xuan; 雲 is the sentence particle, not a second given name Xuanyun.
He sobered into scholarship and stayed home.
By adulthood he had reformed to solemn dignity and cultivated Confucian learning; for several years his feet did not cross the threshold.
The original drops 弱冠, 折節嚴重, 修尚儒學, and 足不逾閾者數年. The replacement restores those facts without adding extras.
He died under Shi rule; cousin Mai continued the line.
In the end he died under the Shi clan; his clansman Zhi's son Mai was appointed heir.
族人峙子邁 is the son Mai of clansman Zhi, appointed heir. 'Cousin Mai' collapses two people and misstates the kinship.
Yi and Gu inherited literary fame.
Xian had two sons, Yi and Gu, both famed for literary talent.
憲有二子：挹、㲄 states that Yi and Gu are Xian's two sons, both famed for literary talent. The original omits the filiation and the count.
When distinguished figures were few, men mostly traded praise of administrative talent—thinking to glorify house and state—is this not precisely what Chen Qian meant!
When distinguished figures were few, men mostly traded praise of administrative talent—thinking to glorify house and state—is this not a description of Chen Qian!
豈陳騫之謂歟 is the idiom 'is this not what is meant of Chen Qian' / a description of him, not a claim that Chen Qian 'meant' the preceding remark.
